paragraphs.text: “My sheep,” says the Life-giver, “hear my voice and follow me, and I give them eternal life.” What else can one expect from Life but life? What other hope can there be of receiving from light than the rays of light? Or what else can one look for from the fountain of benefits than the beneficence of grace? For this reason David too says, “With you is the fountain of life, and in the light of your face we see light.” That light is simple and diffused by nature; it sends out many and varied rays of beneficence. It heals the diverse ailments of souls and restores to health the various pains of bodies, for it is the creator of bodies and souls. As it granted them a single creation, so it also bestows a single healing. And from today's reading we may learn how the fountain of good things holds its beneficence of itself.

“Jesus came again to Cana of Galilee, where he had made the water wine.” Remember yesterday's words: what has been said in bodily terms should not be understood in a bodily way. Jesus came, not by any change in the power of his divinity, but by moving from place to place according to the body. For if, according to the divinity, his nature is unbounded, then he is everywhere; in the body he appears now here, now there, fulfilling the order of the dispensation, not acting by his nature. Jesus came and endured toil; he was wearied, not according to the nature of the divinity, but according to the humanity. “Jesus came,” it says, “and was wearied from the journey.” He was wearied in that which can be wearied, and not in the divinity, which never endures weariness. And the prophet bears witness: “God,” he says, “the eternal, who formed the ends of the earth, will not hunger and will not grow weary.” Yet here it says that he grew weary, that he hungered. “He fasted,” it says, “forty days and forty nights, and afterwards he was hungry”; and it is clear that he hungered when he willed. You see that the divine nature is free of passions, and yet, according to the dispensation, it labours and hungers in the body.

And this is the wonder: he grows weary in order to give rest to the weary: “Come to me, you who are weary, and I will give you rest.” You see now: according to the divinity he gives rest to wearied nature, and according to the dispensation he knows the needs of humanity. Could he not have carried the holy body, which he put on from us for our salvation, through the air, so that it would not suffer weariness? Did he not do something of the kind when he carried the body of Habakkuk from the land of the Palestinians to Babylon in a single instant? He moved a single man, a prophet, from one land to another by the grace of an angel, and the prophet suffered no weariness and felt no labour. And what the hand of an angel could do, could the power of the divine nature not bestow on its own body? But there need and necessity demanded speed, for in Babylon there was no one who feared God to feed Daniel. God saw that the prophet was in distress among the lions for bearing witness to his piety, and by the hand of an angel he snatched up the other prophet and carried him there to that prophet. And see the wonder: it does not say that the angel carried him, but that he took him and set him down there. See the power of the angel; why then do you marvel at the Creator of angels? He lifts and carries the prophet, not by putting a support under his feet and raising him up, but by seizing him by the hair and snatching him away. And we know, brothers, how much the body suffers when it is dragged by the hair; yet the prophet crossed so many regions, travelled so many roads, drawn by the hair, and suffered nothing, and in a single instant he took him and set him down there. For it was the power of an angel, which not only lifted him but also granted lightness to his body. It was a body that was lifted, but it was a spirit that lifted and carried it: “Who makes his angels spirits,” it says.

And do not marvel that a light nature lifted a heavy body. First of all, here in this creation that is visible to us, there are things that are heavy by nature and things that are light by [?]. It does not go by weight, nor by size, but by the nature of the created things, whatever it may be. Why is it that all the great cedars, even if whole forests were cut down and fell into the water, would not sink, while the great sea cannot hold up one little needle or a tiny piece [?] of iron? So it does not go by size or by weight, but by the Creator's art. Yet iron cannot float on the water by itself; it floats on the water by means of something light, and is carried from place to place. People fill great ships with iron and carry it wherever they wish; since the nature of wood is light, the light bears the heavy. Take yet another example. A man cannot swim on the water for many hours, even if he knows the art; since he cannot hold out very long without resting, his arms grow tired, and he is bound to sink.

As with the scorching wind, the root is harmed first and then the branches wither along with it, so it is with piety: if the heart is blinded first, then the fruit of the mouth dries up. However much the heretic's tongue may bluster, the more fruitless it becomes, as the prophet too says: “Ephraim's head is diseased, and the root has withered, and it bears no fruit.” Yet one may often see the forms of piety even among the enemies of piety. There is a multitude in the church, and a multitude among the heretics; there is an altar here, and something called an altar there; true priests here, false priests there; here the Gospel is believed, and there the Gospel is [?] scorned; here the only-begotten Son of God is glorified, and there the only-begotten Son of God is insulted; here the Holy Spirit rejoices over the flock, and there the Holy Spirit is grieved at the unbelief. For when the Holy Spirit sees impiety, he is grieved. That is why Paul too says, “Do not grieve the Holy Spirit, by whom you were sealed for the day of your redemption.”

So when you see the heretic with forms of worship like those of the church, do not be deceived by the appearance, but examine the truth. The magicians of the Egyptians also imitated the works of Moses, but theirs were appearances, not truth. Moses threw his rod on the ground, and it became a serpent; the magicians threw their rods too, and they became serpents. The appearances were the same, but the truth made the difference between them plain, for Moses' rod swallowed up their rods, to show that falsehood is swallowed up by truth. And so that you may know, brother, that every heretical opposition drawn up in battle against the words of the apostles belongs with those magicians, listen to Paul: “Those who want to live godly lives in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. But evil men and sorcerers will advance in wickedness, deceived and deceiving. As Jannes and Jambres opposed Moses, so these also oppose the truth: men corrupt in mind, untried in the faith.”

Pay close attention: he calls the opponents of the word of truth evil men and sorcerers. Why sorcerers? Because they deceive foolish ears, for the words of deceivers are sorcery to those they deceive. For example, brothers, when people scratch their ears because of an itch, the scratching seems pleasant; but when they overdo it, they make sores, and the ears become blocked from the excess. In the same way the words of heretics at first seem soothing to the ears, but afterwards they block up the senses. That is why the apostle too says that in the last times some will fall away from the faith, following the itching of their ears. What is the itching of the ears? Being deceived as if by fables. Everything the heretics have is fables; that is why Paul too says, “They will turn their ears away from the truth and fall headlong into fables.” Into what fables? Those of Arius, of Macedonius, of Montanus, of the Manichaeans, and of others like them; for all of them have broken off into fables and stand opposed to the truth. And he did not speak only of their opposition, but also of their downfall: “But they will not advance, for their folly will be plain to all, as theirs also was.” We have the voice of the apostle as a pledge of warning. The physician of souls stands surety [?] with me to dispel these things [?].

From now on, then, do not let the appearances of the heretics, who mock piety, deceive you. Among the Jews too many had the forms of piety, but there was no zeal for the truth in them. Isaiah likens them to a garden without water and a tree full of leaves on which there is no fruit: “They shall be,” he says, “like a terebinth shedding its leaves, and like a garden without water.” The people of the heretics too is a garden without water; it is not watered by the water of life, of which the Life-giver says, “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture says, rivers of living water will flow from his belly.” Jesus said this about the Holy Spirit, whom those who believed were to receive.

See how they are a garden without water. He did not say “like a garden that has never known water,” but “like one without water.” They say there is a Holy Spirit, but they do not have him; they preach him, but do not enjoy the gifts of the Spirit, for the Holy Spirit does not dwell in ungrateful [?] souls. As long as there is piety in a person, the Holy Spirit dwells there; and when piety departs, the Holy Spirit departs too. Indeed, we must pronounce this verdict: every human soul, after grace, receives either the Holy Spirit or an unclean demon. I do not say that the Holy Spirit works prophecy or apostleship in the person; but if someone does not have faith, then, since faith is the gift of the Spirit, he does not have the Holy Spirit. Even if someone is a humble layman, and indeed one of the very least, and has nothing but faith in Christ, the Holy Spirit is in him: “No one can say Jesus is Lord except by the Holy Spirit.” And the soul must either be enlightened by the Holy Spirit or come under the power of unclean demons. And who is it that says this? When King Saul acted lawlessly and dared to presume upon the forbidden rite, which it was not lawful for him to offer, he who had once put to death the witches and soothsayers then took refuge with the soothsayers himself. And what does Scripture say? “The Spirit of the Lord departed from Saul, and an unclean demon tormented him.”

The heretics are a garden without water, and however many plants they plant, there is no hope in them. Whoever does not follow that voice but his own mind, even if he plants something, it is a plant of unbelief. Isaiah testifies that anyone who does not have the word of God, even if he plants something, it is neither hopeful nor trustworthy. Just as there is a plant of faith, so there is also a plant of unbelief. All the plants of the heretics are plants of unbelief, for they are born of their own reasonings; and every right, evangelical and apostolic glorification of God is a plant of faith and a seed of hope. That is why the Life-giver said of the Jews, “Leave them alone; every plant that my Father has not planted will be uprooted.” And how did the heavenly Father plant? Through prophets and apostles. And how did Satan plant? Through heretics and the impious. Let the plant of impiety be uprooted, and let no place be found for Satan. Everything that opposes the power of Christ and rises up against it is torn down; the darkness that fights against the light is put to flight by the light. But let us come to what lies before us.

The Life-giver reproached the cities: “Woe to you, Chorazin! Woe to you, Bethsaida! For if the mighty works done in you had been done in Tyre and Sidon, they would have repented long ago in sackcloth and ashes.” Let the Gospel say now as well: Woe to you, Arius! Woe to you, Macedonius! Woe to you, Eunomius! For if the preaching that was preached to you had been preached in Sodom, perhaps they would have marvelled at the Saviour, glorified the Benefactor, and recognized the Creator. Truly, brothers, we ought not to be angry with the heretics but to mourn over them. Listen to the Scripture that says, “Mourning for the dead lasts seven days, but for the fool and the impious all the days of his life.” And who is the fool and the senseless one? Let David say: “The fool has said in his heart, There is no God.” Not only the pagan says there is no God, but they do too; for in appearance they say that God exists, but in deed they do not. When the heretic says that Christ is God but does not regard him as God by nature, he says it in words only and denies it in deed. For they say that Christ is God, but not by nature as the Father is, since his nature is one thing and the other's another. When someone denies in heart and mind the honour of the Son's divinity, then even if he says “God,” he does not regard him as God, for he defaces the true image of the Godhead with corrupting colours.

And now, what is to be said about that? As I said before, prophecy was the spring and the Gospel the harvest. But do not let the words I spoke yesterday seem strange to you, that the time of the prophets was the time of spring and sowing, and that of the Gospel the time of summer and harvest; for there is also another harvest. The prophets sowed, and the apostles reaped after the coming of Christ; and again, God sows and the angels reap. Of the prophets' sowing the apostles were the reapers, and of the Life-giver's preaching the angels will be the reapers. The prophets sowed the knowledge of things to come; they also sowed the coming of Christ, heralding it in advance; the apostles of Christ reaped it. Christ sowed beforehand the hope of the resurrection; the prophets also sowed the coming of the Life-giver that was still to be; and Christ too sowed the resurrection of the dead that is to come, and his second coming. And that the apostles were the reapers of the first sowing and the angels will be of the second, the word is his own: “Behold, a sower went out to sow good seed; and tares also sprang up with it.” To cut it short: “At the time of harvest I will say to the reapers, Gather the tares by themselves and the wheat by itself.” When the disciples asked what the parable meant, he said, “The field is the world; the one who sowed is the Son of Man; the good seed are the children of the kingdom; the tares are the children of the evil one; and the harvest is the end of the world.”

And it is not for nothing that Zechariah shows the punishment of the scythe, which the Greek calls a sickle. “I saw,” he says, “a flying scythe. And I said to the angel who was speaking with me, Lord, what is this? And he said, This is the curse that goes out over the face of the whole earth, and it consumes the liar and his house and everything that is his.” Why not a sword, nor a spear or an arrow, but a sickle? Because the sickle is kept for the harvest. The reapers, the angels, are sent out and gather [?]; and there one will see the whole world reaped at once. And from where will they reap? They will pluck them out of the tombs; they will not cut them down, but join together again what has been cut apart. Now bodies are sown like seeds in the fields, as Paul too says: “So it is with the resurrection of the dead: it is sown in corruption and rises without corruption.” And since they were sown in tombs, they will be reaped from the tombs. “The Son of Man,” it says, “will send his angels, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of heaven to the ends of the earth.” You may recognize these words in David: “Gather to him his saints.” They will gather them all and assemble them in one place.

All will rise, but some will be set before the dread tribunal as condemned, and others will be caught up before the Lord as saints. When a king enters, the condemned man does not dare to come into the king's sight, while those who are honoured and esteemed go out to meet him. So too, when the Son of God comes from heaven and appears, the saints are caught up to the heights, and so it will seem that they are coming with him. Just as those who go out to meet a king and return with him seem to have been with him all along, so the saints, when they are caught up to meet the Life-giver, will seem to be coming down from heaven with him. And who is the witness to this? Paul: “For the Lord himself, with a command, at the voice of the archangel and with the trumpet of God, will descend from heaven; and the dead will rise first; then we who are alive will be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air, and so we shall be with the Lord forever.” See: they go out to meet him, and they come with him.

And pay attention to the wonders. In this world those who go out to meet kings go in their own chariots and on their own horses; but the Life-giver himself sends heavenly envoys, not chariots and horses but chariots of cloud, his very own. Why, then, do you marvel that Elijah was taken up in a chariot of fire, and the apostles and the others, one by one, in chariots of cloud? And do not reckon the fiery one more honourable than the one of cloud. In that case, envoys were sent to the prophet, chariots of fire and horses of fire, and he was taken up from earthly things to heaven, whirled up from below into the heights like a wheel. Then the chariots were rightly fiery, but afterwards not fiery but of cloud. Why? Because at that time the heavenly vessel still had some earthly needs, so that it had to be renewed by the chariots of fire, to cast off earthly heaviness and take on angelic lightness, since from then on he was to dwell with the angels. There the envoy was of fire, here the envoy is of cloud; for bodies rise without corruption, and so they go up lightly into the cloud. And so that it may not seem that we disparage the one and esteem the other: I said that the prophet was honoured with chariots of fire, and that those who are caught up to meet Christ ascend in clouds, because clouds are the chariots of the holy God. Listen to David: “Who established his upper chambers on the waters, and set his course in the clouds.” With his own chariots he honours the saints. Listen to Isaiah: “Behold, the Lord is seated on a swift cloud, and he will come to Egypt.” You see that he commands the saints to be honoured with his own chariots and to go out to meet the Life-giver.

And how will they go up? He himself makes it plain, for Paul never speaks on his own account, as he says: “You seek proof of Christ who speaks in me.” And what does he say? “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord in the air.” And so some are caught up, while others will be set before the dread tribunal, as the Life-giver himself says: “Amen, I say to you, when the Son of Man comes, if there are two in one bed, one will be taken and the other left; and if two are grinding at one mill, one will be taken up and the other left.” And the apostles say to him, “Where, Lord?” And the Lord says, “Where the body is, there the eagles will be gathered.” Why eagles? Because they are to be caught up into the heights. What does it mean, that there are two in one bed, and one is taken and the other left; and two grinding at one mill, and one is taken up and the other remains? Nothing here is said figuratively, one thing standing for another; the meaning is plain. Scripture calls the ease of this world a bed, and the extreme hardship of those who toil a mill: like men at a mill they go round and round, dizzied amid all kinds of afflictions, from groan to groan, from poverty to poverty. And that Scripture calls extreme hardship a mill, let Moses testify. He says, “The angel went out and struck the firstborn of the Egyptians, from the firstborn of Pharaoh, who sat on the throne of the kingdom, to the firstborn of the captive who was at the mill.” That is why Isaiah too spoke reproachfully to the ruler of the Babylonians: “You said, I am, and I shall remain forever” (that is, I shall reign forever); “therefore childlessness will come upon you. Take the millstones and grind flour.” For he had said, I shall hold dominion and kingship forever and shall never know widowhood; and God brings him down from the throne of the kingdom and binds him to the mill: “Take the millstones,” he says, “grind flour, cross the river” (that is, you will wander about in misery, stumbling). And since the bed is ease and the mill is toil, the Life-giver makes it clear that both among those who do not toil and among those who live at ease some will be righteous and some sinners. Two will be in a bed: the one who is worthy of the faith will be taken up, and the other left to the demons. “And two,” he says, “will be grinding at one mill; one will be taken up and the other will remain.” With the same thought the disciples asked, saying, “Lord, where will they be taken up?” He says to them, “Where my body is,” that is, “where my coming is.”

And he rightly said “the body,” for he is to be revealed in the body. Although the body was covered by the divinity and dyed with the immortal dye, which is wholly immortality, it did not lose its form; the form of the body remains, dyed and steeped in life. Let us offer an illustration of this. Though it is dim and obscure, still from the small one may gain at least some faint sign of the great. Take iron and plunge it into the furnace of fire, and see what it was like before it was plunged into the fire: dark in appearance, cold to the touch. After entering the fire it is bright to look at and hot to the touch; yet it has not ceased to be iron, but has received something beyond its own nature. Though it has become radiant, it has not departed from its own shape: whatever shape you plunge in, that same shape appears, whether round or triangular or square or whatever it may be; it does not change its shape, but its colour takes on the colour of fire. In the same way the holy and adorable body of the Lord was dyed with the immortal dye of godliness and steeped in life, and it has put on the divinity, not merely on the outside, but like the iron, within and without. Yet it remains in its incorruptible form, to the glory of believers and the shame of those who scorn him.

Have you never seen how, when people return from a foreign land after a long time, their families look for a sign, not of any glory, even if they come back in glory, but of their former life, to see whether this is truly the same person? They do not look so closely at the clothes as at the shape of the brows, the marks on the hands, and the hair, whether it is thin [?] or curly; and the body's blemishes become heralds of the one no longer recognized. That is why he wishes to save [?] the saints not by his divinity but in the form of his body, so that they may look and see that it is truly he who was disbelieved by Caiaphas, judged by Pilate, and went up on the cross; so that the sight may bear witness against the war waged on God, and the glory may reveal the truth. Consider how Peter will exult, and the apostles will join in a dance and go about saying to one another: “This is our God; this is he who was once crucified among us; this is he who was once despised for our sake. See his form; look at his eyes.”

And who foretold this? Isaiah. “It shall be,” he says, “in the last days that they will say, ‘Behold our God, in whom we hoped,’ and they will rejoice, and eye will see eye, when the Lord has mercy on Zion”—which is to say that he will appear openly, right before their eyes. The righteous rejoice and recognize their Lord; the wicked mourn when they recognize the one whom they despised. For if here in this world someone has wronged another, and has himself fallen from honor, and then sees the one he wronged in a position of power, he is anxious and trembles that the man may remember what was done to him, that he may call the insult to mind; and he devises every kind of scheme to calm his anger: whether he can win him over himself, or through friends. But how will you be able to win over your Lord? Through the martyrs, whom you slandered, or through the apostles, whom you dishonored? You defiled their names—Matthew and Bartholomew—saying, “What do they have to do with Plato? What comparison is there between them and Aristotle?” Now you despise their names, and then you will run to take shelter under their intercession—with what eyes, with what boldness? No, you cannot hope to win him over. Will you then take to flight? And do you not hear David: “Where shall I go from your spirit, or where shall I flee from your face?” And if there is no flight anywhere, O wretched and miserable one, learn to flee to him as a fugitive. Just as those who realize that they will not escape the tortures of the judges, since the law demands what is due, have only one refuge left to flee to: to turn to the king, and by royal grace to dispel the punishment of torture. For this reason David too, aware of the burden of sins that tormented him, and knowing that by the commands of the law he deserved punishment, flees from everyone and takes refuge in the Lord alone: “You, Lord, are my hope and my refuge.”

Just as the righteous will rejoice when they see Christ, so those who are transgressors will be broken-hearted; and even before their punishment, at the sight of the holy face, they will be undone and fall down when they see the sign of the Crucified, of which the Life-giver himself said: “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” Before Christ appears, the cross comes first, with exceedingly bright light and intense rays, which drowns the sun, covers the moon and extinguishes the stars. First the sign appears, and then the king. Just as here the standards appear first and then the king comes, so there too the cross first appears in light, and then Christ is revealed; so that when they see the cross they may be ashamed that what once seemed a thing of reproach now comes from on high with honor. And the standard-bearers will not be the apostles, nor the prophets, but archangels and hosts of angels; they will come before the cross and with the cross.

And after saying, “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven,” what does he say? “Then all the tribes of the earth will mourn.” Bitter mourning will come upon the unbelievers, just as great joy upon the believers. And not only did the Life-giver say this, but first the prophet Zechariah: “Then the sun will go down upon the prophets, and the moon will be darkened. Then they will look on him whom they pierced”—that is, the one whom they fastened to the cross with nails. “Then the tribes will mourn each by itself: the tribe of the house of David by itself, and their wives by themselves; the tribe of the house of Nathan by itself, and their wives by themselves; every tribe by itself, and their wives by themselves.” Why does he speak of all the tribes, and why does he mention David and Nathan? Nathan was not one of the patriarchs, but was of the line of David. David had two eminent sons; although he had many, two were especially honored, Solomon and Nathan. From Nathan descends the line of Joseph, and from Solomon comes the line of Mary. Mary was of royal descent, and Joseph, though also of royal descent, was not from Solomon, who took the throne of David, but from Nathan, the king's brother. And since the reproach of having fought against God was to fall upon all, and most of all upon the kinsmen who did not recognize their own Savior, he says, “The tribe of David will mourn by itself”; for since Christ was from David according to the flesh, his kinsmen mourn at what a pledge of salvation they have lost.

And now, so that we may not mourn but share in the rejoicing, and receive the Crucified in glory—let the Jews hear this, who put the body of the Son of God on the cross, and the heretics, who despised his divinity. The books of the prophets and of the apostles are to be opened before the tribunal of Christ. Do you think the prophets will not come to the tribunal, and that the Jews will not stand bowed before the judgment seat of Christ, and the heretics stricken and broken-hearted at the dread judgment? The Jews will be asked, “Why did you deny him?” The heretics will be asked, “Why did you blaspheme?” And what answer will they be able to give? Perhaps the Jew will say, “I heard from the prophets: ‘I am God, and besides me there is no other god; I am the first and I am the last.’ We learned this from the prophet Isaiah; and what could we wretched people do?” And he will say to the heretics, “And why did you blaspheme the Son? Why did you insult the glory of the Only-begotten?” Perhaps they too will say, “Peter taught us so, and Paul instructed us so: that ‘Christ is our peace, who made both one,’ and reconciled us to the Father as mediator between God and men. He preached him as mediator, and not as God—and we were deceived.”

Then the hosts of the prophets will grow angry, and the ranks of the apostles will be indignant; they will bring their books into the midst. Isaiah, opening his book, will say: “See, Lord, how I became the advocate of your anointing. Let the oracles be read which I spoke concerning you; let the Jews hear, and let the Christians say whether the apostles preached anything more than I did. Did I not know you, the only-begotten Son of God? Did I not proclaim beforehand, ‘A child is born to us, a son is given to us, and his name is called Angel of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, God, Mighty, Powerful, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come’? Did I not join together the teaching about his divinity and the teaching about the economy? At one point: ‘God, Mighty, Powerful, Prince of Peace’; at another: ‘Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Emmanuel,’ which translated means ‘God with us.’ Did I not also proclaim the passion: that ‘like a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and for the sins of the people he was handed over to death’? Did I not also proclaim his coming? Did I say that a prophet was to come, and not God? Just as the prophet Zechariah said, ‘Say to the daughter of Zion, Behold, your king comes, riding on a colt,’ so I too said, ‘Behold, the Lord comes with power.’ None of the apostles was a herald for you as I was. They preached you together with your body, and gave the ignorant occasion for blasphemy; but I proclaimed your divinity in full: Angel of Great Counsel, God, Mighty, Powerful, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come. None of your apostles said this. I was your herald before the apostles; let no one slander my writings.” Isaiah says this with a fervent mind, for he is bold and impartial, as the Apostle also says: “Isaiah is very bold and says.”

Moses too comes forward, who was dearer and more honored by the Jews than God; stepping into the midst, he too becomes an advocate. He begins to say, “Wretched and miserable ones”—for Moses has a different character; he rebukes with gentleness. “The man Moses,” it says, “was meeker than all the sons of men.” “Did I not foretell long ago the barrenness of your unbelief? Since you could not receive great things, I said, ‘The Lord God will raise up for you a prophet from your own nation; him you shall hear. And every soul that does not hear that prophet shall utterly perish.’ And if you thought this something small, did I not proclaim the Trinity at the very beginning of the account of creation? At one point: ‘God said, Let there be light’; at another: ‘Let us make man according to the likeness of the image of our form’; and at another: ‘Come, let us go down and divide the tongues.’ Did I not write with my own hands, ‘The Lord rained fire and brimstone from the Lord upon the people of Sodom and Gomorrah’? Do I not grieve at your perdition? But I think it better to disregard you, and not to turn my face toward you there [?].” And who is the witness of these words? The Lord himself, who said of the Jews: “Do you think that I will be your accuser before the Father? There is one who accuses you: Moses, in whom you have boasted. For if you believed Moses, you would also believe me; for he wrote about me.” And that books are to be opened, Daniel bears witness: “I saw that the Ancient of Days sat, and his throne was like fire; I saw that thrones were set in place, and books were opened.” All this they will say concerning the Jews.

The heretics will be called into the midst. Let Paul stand forward as their accuser, he who was slandered by their godless tongues. They too will be asked, “Where did you read that the Son is spoken of as lower than the Father?” And they say, “You and Peter taught it. He said, ‘Exalted at the right hand of God, and having received the promise of the Spirit, he poured it out on us’; and again, ‘Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit’; and, ‘God made this Jesus both Lord and Christ.’ And you said, ‘of God the Father, who raised him from the dead’; and again, ‘I thank God through Jesus Christ’—and you did not say, ‘I thank him,’ but ‘Through him I thank God.’” Then Paul will open his mouth, which was never shut—he who said, “Our mouth is open to you, Corinthians”—and he will rebuke them: “Son of lawlessness, evil seed, plant of unbelief, did I not proclaim the divinity of the Only-begotten? Did I not say, ‘Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever’? Did I not say, ‘He did not count it robbery to be equal with God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant’? Did I not say, ‘Neither barbarian nor savage nor Scythian, but Christ is all and in all’? Did I not say, ‘He who is the radiance of glory and the imprint of being and the image of the invisible God, who bears all things by his power’?” And they say, “Did you not preach him as a man? Did you not preach Christ according to the flesh?” “But I who preached Christ according to the flesh also said elsewhere, ‘Even though we once knew Christ according to the flesh, from now on we know him so no longer.’” Coming forward, Peter too will say: “You read of my condescension to the Gentiles and to the Jews; did you not read the great confession with which I confessed Christ? For what confession did I receive the keys? For calling Jesus a Nazarene? No, but because I said, ‘You are the Christ, the Son of the living God.’ When I said that God made him Lord and Christ, was I speaking of the time when he was begotten as offspring of the Father [?]?”

And now, be on your guard, for books and records are to be opened; and the King will sit; and the advocates of the truth will come forward, and the accusers will be put to shame. Let us act in advance, before the tribunal. Before the King sits to judge, it is possible to win the Judge over; before the tribunal one may entreat; before the dread judgment seat there is no room to plead. May it be granted to all of us to appear blameless before the judgment seat of Christ, for his are the glory and the power forever. Amen.
